topic: Explain the Concepts of systemd Units and Targets
prompt: What PID does systemd run as?
options: Whatever the kernel assigns at boot
explanation: The kernel starts systemd as PID 1 after the switch-root, and it stays running until shutdown, managing initialization, services and process tracking.

topic: Explain the Concepts of systemd Units and Targets
prompt: Which directory holds the default unit files distributed with installed packages?
explanation: Packages install their units in /usr/lib/systemd/system — the lowest precedence. Runtime units in /run/systemd/system override those, and administrator customisations under /etc/systemd override both.

topic: Explain the Concepts of systemd Units and Targets
prompt: Which of these are valid systemd unit types? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Unit types include automount, device, mount, path, scope, service, slice, socket, swap, target and timer. Runlevels are the System V concept that targets replaced.

topic: Explain the Concepts of systemd Units and Targets
prompt: What is the difference between the Requires and Wants directives in a unit file?
options: Requires makes the unit fail if the dependency does not start; Wants does not
Wants is checked first, then Requires
Requires applies to targets and Wants to services
explanation: Wants is the softer form — activation proceeds even if the wanted unit fails. Before and After express ordering, and Conflicts names units that must NOT be running.

topic: Explain the Concepts of systemd Units and Targets
prompt: What is a systemd target?
options: A logical grouping of units used to bring the system to an operational state
A single service and its dependencies
A configuration file for the kernel
explanation: Targets are a unit type with the .target extension. Some inherit services from other targets and add their own — graphical.target, for example, builds on multi-user.target.

topic: Manage systemd Services and Targets
prompt: Check the current status of the atd service.
explanation: status shows the description, load state, whether the unit is enabled for autostart, the activation state and the main PID.

topic: Manage systemd Services and Targets
prompt: Configure the httpd service to start automatically at boot and start it right now, in a single command.
explanation: --now combines enable with start (and disable with stop). Without it, enable only affects future boots and start only affects the current one.

topic: Manage systemd Services and Targets
prompt: Check whether the atd service is configured to start automatically at boot.
explanation: is-enabled reports the autostart setting, is-active reports whether it is currently running, and is-failed reports whether it crashed.

topic: Manage systemd Services and Targets
prompt: How does masking a unit differ from disabling it?
options: Masking symlinks the unit to /dev/null so it cannot be started at all, even manually
Masking only prevents autostart; disabling also stops it
explanation: A disabled unit will not autostart but can still be started by hand or pulled in as a dependency. A masked unit cannot be started at all until you unmask it.

topic: Manage systemd Services and Targets
prompt: What is the difference between systemctl reload and systemctl restart?
options: reload makes the running unit re-read its configuration without changing its PID; restart stops and starts it
restart re-reads configuration; reload stops and starts
They are equivalent for service units
explanation: reload avoids dropping connections because the process is never replaced. Use daemon-reload — a different subcommand — after editing unit files, to make systemd re-read them.

topic: Manage systemd Services and Targets
prompt: After editing a unit file on disk, make systemd re-read all unit files and rebuild the dependency tree.
explanation: Without daemon-reload, systemd keeps using the version of the unit it loaded into memory earlier, and your edits appear to have no effect.

topic: Display and Configure Default System Boot Target
prompt: Show which target the system boots into by default.
explanation: default.target is a symbolic link to the real target file. get-default reports where that link points.

topic: Display and Configure Default System Boot Target
prompt: Persistently change the default boot target to the text-based multi-user target.
explanation: set-default replaces the default.target symlink so the change survives reboots. This is distinct from isolate, which only switches the currently running system.

topic: Switch to Non-Default Targets for Testing or Troubleshooting
prompt: Switch the currently running system from the graphical target to the multi-user target, without rebooting.
explanation: isolate transitions the running system to the named target, stopping units that are not part of it. It is temporary — the default boot target is unchanged.

topic: Switch to Non-Default Targets for Testing or Troubleshooting
prompt: How do the rescue and emergency targets differ?
options: rescue mounts local file systems with networking disabled; emergency mounts only / read-only with no other services
emergency includes networking; rescue does not
rescue requires no password; emergency does
They are the same target under two names
explanation: Emergency is the more minimal of the two — root read-only, nothing else mounted, no networking or services. Both prompt for the root password.

topic: Switch to Non-Default Targets for Testing or Troubleshooting
prompt: What are the halt, poweroff and reboot commands in RHEL 10?
options: Symbolic links to systemctl, kept for compatibility
explanation: They map to `shutdown -H now`, `-P now` and `-r now` respectively, broadcasting a warning, blocking new logins and stopping services first. Using systemctl directly is recommended.

topic: Analyze System Log Configuration File
prompt: Which daemon handles traditional system logging, and which file configures it?
explanation: rsyslogd reads /etc/rsyslog.conf plus any .conf files in /etc/rsyslog.d at startup, and writes most logs under /var/log.

topic: Analyze System Log Configuration File
prompt: In an rsyslog rule, what do the two halves of the selector field mean?
options: facility.priority — the category of process, and the severity level
priority.facility — the severity, and the destination
file.action — the log file and what to do with it
source.target — where the message came from and where it goes
explanation: Facilities include auth, authpriv, cron, daemon, kern, mail and local0–local7. A named priority also matches every higher severity, so mail.error logs error, crit, alert and emerg.

topic: Analyze System Log Configuration File
prompt: Which is the correct order of syslog priorities from most to least critical?
options: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug
debug, info, notice, warning, err, crit, alert, emerg
crit, emerg, alert, err, warning, info, notice, debug
alert, emerg, crit, warning, err, notice, info, debug
explanation: emerg means the system is unusable and debug is the most verbose. Specifying a priority captures that level and everything more severe.

topic: Analyze System Log Configuration File
prompt: Which log files receive the described messages by default? (Select all that apply.)
options: /var/log/boot.log — boot messages from the local7 facility
explanation: /var/log/messages catches all info-and-above messages EXCEPT the mail, authpriv and cron facilities, which have their own files.

topic: Examine Log Rotation Settings
prompt: Which files configure log rotation, and what triggers it?
explanation: logrotate.timer invokes logrotate.service daily. The global default in logrotate.conf is weekly rotation with four weeks retained; per-service files in /etc/logrotate.d override those globals.

topic: Record Custom Messages in System Log File
prompt: Write the custom message "Hello world" into the system log.
explanation: The imuxsock input module in rsyslog.conf provides this support. Entries default to user.notice priority; -p sets a different facility.priority. Normal users may run logger.

topic: Retrieve, Filter, and Scrutinize Log Messages from systemd Journal
prompt: Show journal messages from the current boot only.
explanation: -b defaults to -0, the current boot. -1 is the previous boot, -2 the one before that, and so on.

topic: Retrieve, Filter, and Scrutinize Log Messages from systemd Journal
prompt: Show only the journal entries belonging to the sshd.service unit.
explanation: -u filters by systemd unit. Other useful filters are -k for kernel messages, -n for a line count, -p for priority, -f to follow live, and -o verbose for full detail.

topic: Configure Persistent Journal Storage to Maintain Log Data Across System Reboots
prompt: Where does systemd-journald store journals by default, and why are they lost at reboot?
options: /run/log/journal — /run is a memory-based file system destroyed at shutdown
/tmp/journal — files there are deleted after 10 days
explanation: /run is created in memory at boot and destroyed at shutdown, so journals there are transient. rsyslogd reads them and writes durable text copies to /var/log/messages.

topic: Configure Persistent Journal Storage to Maintain Log Data Across System Reboots
prompt: With Storage=auto (the default) in journald.conf, what must you do to get persistent journals?
options: Set Storage=volatile and restart the service
Add a logrotate rule for the journal
explanation: auto uses /var/log/journal if it exists but will not create it; persistent creates it for you. After restarting the service, a subdirectory named for the machine ID in /etc/machine-id appears.

topic: Apply and Manage Tuning Profiles to Enhance System Performance
prompt: List the available tuning profiles along with the currently active one.
explanation: tuned-adm active shows only the current profile. The default profile on a typical RHEL system is balanced.

topic: Apply and Manage Tuning Profiles to Enhance System Performance
prompt: Switch the active tuning profile to powersave.
explanation: tuned-adm recommend suggests the best profile for this system's characteristics, and tuned-adm off disables tuning entirely until you set a profile again.

topic: Apply and Manage Tuning Profiles to Enhance System Performance
prompt: Where must a custom tuning profile be stored for tuned to recognise it?
explanation: Predefined profiles ship in /usr/lib/tuned/profiles, one subdirectory per profile. Custom profiles — written from scratch or based on an existing one — belong under /etc/tuned.

topic: Apply and Manage Tuning Profiles to Enhance System Performance
prompt: Which tuning profile provides maximum performance at the cost of maximum power consumption?
explanation: balanced trades the two off and is the usual default; powersave and balanced-battery favour power saving; virtual-guest and virtual-host are tuned for virtualisation.
